strengths: Addresses an important practical limitation of equilibrium propagation: slow settling dynamics and unstable training. Feedback scaling is a simple intervention with little implementation overhead.
Provides useful empirical analysis across feedback strengths, network depths, symmetric and asymmetric connections, including convergence diagnostics and five-run statistics.

Residual connections substantially improve the reported ten-layer results: MNIST accuracy increases from 92.49% to 97.52%, and Fashion-MNIST from 81.67% to 88.47%. Shallow models also achieve accuracy comparable to the tested BP baselines.
weaknesses: Novelty is insufficiently established relative to the acknowledged literature on weak-feedback contrastive Hebbian learning, local representation alignment, and skip connections for credit assignment. The paper primarily combines these existing ideas without direct comparisons demonstrating a distinctive advantage. More recent EP methods cited in the paper are also absent from the experimental baselines.

The headline speedup comparisons are substantially confounded. Table 1 changes batch size, optimizer, activation, and sometimes training duration alongside feedback scaling. The closer Ours-DLR comparison reduces approximately 8:27 to 1:01, about 8.3-fold, while still changing the activation and learning formulation; it does not substantiate the claim of at least an order-of-magnitude improvement from feedback regulation alone. Matched implementations and time-to-target-accuracy comparisons are needed.

Evaluation is restricted to MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, small fully connected networks, and a shallow convolutional model. This does not support claims about practical large-scale EP. The ten-layer experiments use 64 units per layer, and no corresponding runtime evaluation establishes that residual connections retain the advertised speed advantage.

The BP-equivalence argument is considerably narrower than the implemented method. Appendix equations S13–S15 introduce a feedback-dependent normalization absent from Algorithm 1 and assume transposed feedback weights and infinitesimal feedback and nudging. They do not establish gradient correctness for finite feedback, fixed asymmetric weights, or arbitrary residual graphs. Likewise, weak perturbations do not by themselves justify dropping the activation derivative from the stated LRA objective's gradient.

The convergence discussion overstates what the spectral radius establishes. For general nonlinear asymmetric dynamics, a weight-matrix spectral radius below one is not by itself a global convergence guarantee; appropriate Jacobian or contraction conditions are needed. The manuscript does not establish such conditions throughout training or for its arbitrary graph architectures, and its Lyapunov diagnostics sample a limited trajectory.

Residual and arbitrary-graph comparisons lack controls for the added connections and capacity. BP and FA are not evaluated with matching residual topologies, so the reported improvements do not isolate an advantage of the proposed learning rule. Comparisons against layerwise learning-rate compensation and direct feedback would also clarify the mechanism.

Reproducibility is undermined by substantive specification errors. Algorithm S2 uses free-phase states throughout the clamped-phase recurrent inputs, which as written prevents the nudging signal from propagating to the first hidden layer. The hard-sigmoid definition is identically one, and the description of fixed feedback weights is ambiguous for experiments requiring maintained symmetry. Although these may be transcription errors, the empty code-availability statement leaves no implementation to resolve them.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful limitation of equilibrium propagation: slow settling and unstable recurrent dynamics. Feedback scaling is simple and inexpensive to implement.
Provides useful ablations across feedback strength, depth, symmetric/asymmetric connections, and iteration budgets, with five-run statistics and supplementary dynamical analyses.

Demonstrates substantial improvements from skip connections: the symmetric 10-layer model improves from 92.49% to 97.52% on MNIST and from 81.67% to 88.47% on Fashion-MNIST, approaching the reported BP baselines.
weaknesses: Novelty is insufficiently established. The paper acknowledges prior work combining weak feedback with fast convergence and BP approximation, and LRA methods using weak feedback and skip connections. It lacks direct comparisons demonstrating a substantive advance over these closely related approaches or newer EP methods.

The headline speedups are confounded. Table 1 changes activation functions, optimizers, batch sizes, and sometimes training epochs alongside feedback scaling. The better-controlled Ours-DLR comparison still changes activation and yields approximately 8.3× acceleration, below the claimed minimum order-of-magnitude improvement. The provenance and comparability of timings for literature-derived P-EP results also need clarification.

Evaluation is limited to MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, with small fully connected networks and a shallow convolutional model. This does not substantiate claims about practical large-scale EP. Deep residual models are evaluated with long settling budgets rather than demonstrating that depth, competitive accuracy, and rapid convergence are achieved together.

The theoretical argument has a narrower scope than the claims. The appendix recovers feedforward BP in a joint weak-feedback/weak-nudging limit with symmetric weights and an additional update normalization absent from the main algorithm. It does not establish gradient correctness for finite feedback, fixed asymmetric connections, or arbitrary residual graphs. Likewise, weight-matrix spectral radius alone is not a general convergence guarantee for nonlinear recurrent dynamics.

Residual and arbitrary-graph comparisons lack architecture-matched BP and FA controls. Adding connections changes capacity and credit-assignment path lengths, so outperforming a plain FA network does not isolate an advantage of the proposed learning method.

Reproducibility is compromised by concrete specification problems. The code-availability statement has no link. Algorithm S2 uses free-phase states throughout its clamped-phase recurrent computations; taken literally, the first hidden layer cannot respond to nudging. The stated hard-sigmoid formula is also constant-valued. These issues require correction and verification against the implementation.

Biological and hardware benefits remain largely motivational: symmetric variants retain weight transport, most experiments use Adam, and no physical implementation or noise/precision robustness evaluation supports the proposed hardware advantages.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful limitation of equilibrium propagation: slow, unstable settling. Feedback scaling is simple and inexpensive to implement.
Provides useful sweeps over feedback strength, network depth, and iteration count, supplemented by convergence diagnostics and five-run accuracy statistics.
Residual connections substantially improve ten-layer performance: MNIST accuracy increases from 92.49% to 97.52%, and Fashion-MNIST from 81.67% to 88.47%, approaching the reported BP baselines.
Includes symmetric and asymmetric networks, convolutional experiments, pseudocode, and optimizer details.
weaknesses: Novelty is insufficiently established relative to acknowledged prior work on weak-feedback contrastive Hebbian learning, local representation alignment, and skip connections. Comparisons omit recent EP methods and LRA, which are particularly relevant to the claimed advances.

The headline speedups are confounded by changes in optimizer, batch size, activation, and sometimes training epochs. The more controlled Ours-DLR comparison still changes activation and achieves approximately 8.3× acceleration, below the claimed minimum order-of-magnitude improvement. The provenance of baseline wall-clock measurements also needs clarification.

Evaluation is restricted to MNIST and Fashion-MNIST with small networks. This does not establish practicality for large-scale AI, and the ten-layer experiments retain 100 free-phase and 50 clamped-phase iterations without reporting their runtime.

Residual and arbitrary-graph models are compared against BP/FA models without matching skip connections or parameter budgets. Consequently, the results do not isolate an advantage of the learning method from the benefit of the architecture.

The theoretical support is limited to an infinitesimal, symmetric, two-hidden-layer setting with additional update normalization absent from the main algorithm. It does not establish gradient fidelity for the finite-feedback, asymmetric, or arbitrary-graph experiments. Weight-matrix spectral radius below one is also not a general guarantee of global convergence for nonlinear recurrent dynamics without additional conditions.

Reproducibility is impaired by substantive pseudocode inconsistencies. Algorithm S2 uses free-phase states throughout the clamped recurrence, preventing hidden-layer perturbations from propagating as described. The stated hard-sigmoid formula is identically one, and feedback weights are described both as fixed and as symmetric with changing forward weights. These issues require correction and implementation clarification.
Biological and hardware implications exceed the evidence: no physical implementation, energy measurements, or robustness evaluation under hardware noise and limited precision is provided.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful limitation of equilibrium propagation: slow settling and unstable training. Feedback attenuation is simple to implement, and the experiments consistently demonstrate its convergence–credit-assignment tradeoff.
Provides useful ablations across feedback strength, network depth, symmetry, residual connections, numerical precision, and noise, with five-run statistics for the principal accuracy comparisons.

Residual connections substantially improve the 10-layer model: MNIST accuracy increases from 92.49% to 97.49%, and CIFAR-10 accuracy from 34.90% to 44.46%. The shallow convolutional model also approaches its matched BP baseline.
weaknesses: Novelty is insufficiently established relative to the acknowledged literature on weak-feedback contrastive Hebbian learning, local representation alignment, and skip connections for credit assignment. The paper does not clearly demonstrate what new principle or capability emerges beyond combining these established ideas.

The headline orders-of-magnitude speedup is confounded. Table 1 compares published P-EP results against runs with different activations, optimizers, batch sizes, and sometimes epoch counts; a common hardware and implementation basis is not established. The closer Ours-DLR comparison gives approximately 8.3× acceleration, still changes activation, and does not justify attributing the much larger gains solely to feedback regulation.

Evaluation is limited to MNIST and CIFAR-10 with small fully connected networks and shallow CNNs. Comparisons omit the more recent EP methods cited by the paper, including gradient-bias reduction and Jacobian homeostasis. Deep CNN scalability remains untested, and the deep fully connected models retain substantial gaps to BP.

The theoretical support is narrower than the claimed EP–BP equivalence. Appendix C derives a weak-feedback, weak-nudging limit for a two-hidden-layer symmetric network and introduces feedback-dependent normalization absent from the implemented update. It does not establish gradient correctness at the finite feedback strengths used experimentally, for arbitrary asymmetric graphs, or for the residual architectures. Initial-batch cosine similarities provide only limited validation.

Residual comparisons do not include BP and FA trained with the same added skip connections and parameter counts. Consequently, improved accuracy cannot be cleanly separated from the increased capacity and generally easier optimization of the modified architecture.

Claims of hardware practicality and remarkable noise resilience exceed the evidence. No physical implementation or energy measurement is provided, while Figure S12 shows five-layer accuracy falling from about 97.6% to 81.4% at state-noise intensity 0.001. The precision experiments further expose the fragility of weak credit signals.

Several reporting ambiguities impede reproducibility: Section 3.2 states that feedback weights remain fixed, whereas the symmetric experiments require clarification about maintaining transpose symmetry; convergence stopping criteria are unspecified; and no validation-based hyperparameter or checkpoint-selection protocol is described despite extensive test-accuracy sweeps and reporting of maximum test accuracy.

strengths: Addresses a relevant bottleneck in equilibrium propagation: slow, unstable settling. Feedback-strength sweeps and dynamical diagnostics provide evidence that weaker feedback improves convergence.

Achieves accuracy comparable to matched shallow BP models, including 75.04% versus 75.45% on CIFAR-10 with convolutional networks. Most principal experiments report five-run means and standard deviations.

Residual connections substantially improve the 10-layer model over its non-residual counterpart. The appendix includes useful gradient-alignment, frozen-layer, and noise experiments, alongside training details and pseudocode.
weaknesses: Novelty is insufficiently established relative to weak-feedback contrastive Hebbian learning, LRA, and existing EP acceleration methods. The paper acknowledges that weak feedback can approximate BP and accelerate convergence, but does not convincingly establish what combining this principle with standard skip connections adds beyond prior approaches. Direct comparisons with these closely related methods are missing.

The headline orders-of-magnitude speedup is confounded. Table 1 changes batch size, optimizer, activation, and sometimes epoch count relative to the historical P-EP baseline. The closer 3-layer SGD comparison reduces runtime from 8:27 to 1:01, approximately 8.3 times, while still changing activation and other formulation details. Consistently controlled implementations and time-to-matched-accuracy measurements are needed to attribute the claimed gains to feedback regulation.

Evaluation does not establish practical scalability. Experiments cover only MNIST and CIFAR-10, with deep models restricted to narrow fully connected networks. On CIFAR-10, residual models remain below BP at 10 layers (44.46% versus 48.23%) and 20 layers (43.61% versus 47.35%). The arbitrary-graph model reaches only 30.94% with substantial variability. These results support a narrower claim than broadly practical deep EP.

The theoretical treatment supports a restricted limiting relationship, not general equivalence of the implemented updates to BP. Appendix C assumes symmetric feedback, infinitesimal feedback and nudging, and introduces layer-dependent normalization absent from the main update rule. It does not establish gradient correctness for finite feedback, fixed asymmetric feedback, or the residual graph models. Gradient-direction similarity on one batch is also insufficient to establish equivalence throughout training.

Important controls are missing for the residual contribution: Table 2 does not report BP or FA with matched residual connectivity, parameter-matched alternatives, or a 20-layer non-residual EP baseline. Consequently, architectural capacity gains and improvements specific to the proposed credit-assignment method are not cleanly separated.

Biological and hardware claims exceed the evidence. The strongest results retain transpose-related feedback weights, leaving weight transport unresolved, and no physical implementation or energy measurement is presented. Appendix C additionally exposes sensitivity to floating-point precision and state noise at depth, which deserves greater weight in the practicality claims.

Several specification issues reduce confidence in reproducibility and technical precision. The text does not clearly reconcile fixed feedback weights with maintained symmetric feedback; Appendix D defines hard-sigmoid as max(min(x, 0), 1), which is constant; and Algorithm S3 appears to reset clamped states inside every iteration. The blanket statement that adjacency spectral radius below one guarantees nonlinear convergence also requires additional assumptions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical limitation of equilibrium propagation: slow and unstable settling dynamics. Feedback attenuation is simple to implement, and the experiments consistently demonstrate its tradeoff between convergence speed and credit-signal strength.
Shallow-network results are encouraging. The convolutional model achieves 75.04% ± 0.51% on CIFAR-10 versus 75.45% ± 0.46% for BP, and several MNIST configurations also closely match BP.
Residual connections substantially improve the 10-layer symmetric model: MNIST accuracy rises from 92.49% to 97.49%, and CIFAR-10 accuracy from 34.90% to 44.46%.

The supplementary analyses provide useful depth, including feedback-strength sweeps, dynamical diagnostics, gradient similarity, frozen-layer controls, numerical-precision effects, and noise sensitivity. Main results include five repetitions and reported variability.
weaknesses: The contribution is insufficiently differentiated from closely related work. The discussion explicitly acknowledges that weak feedback already accelerates contrastive Hebbian learning and approximates BP, and that LRA combines weak feedback with skip connections. Applying these principles to vector-field EP is plausible, but direct comparisons with these methods are missing. Comparisons with more recent EP methods, including the cited 2021 and 2024 approaches, are also needed.

The central orders-of-magnitude speedup claim is confounded. Table 1 changes batch size, optimizer, activation, and sometimes epoch count alongside feedback scaling, while P-EP results are attributed to prior work. The closer 3-layer SGD comparison reduces runtime from 8:27 to 1:01, approximately 8.3-fold, and still changes the activation and learning formulation. A controlled implementation on identical hardware with matched training settings is needed to isolate the claimed benefit. Separate inference-speed measurements are absent.

Evidence for practical deep-network scaling remains limited. Evaluation covers only MNIST and CIFAR-10, with deep experiments using narrow fully connected networks. Even with residual connections, the 10-layer CIFAR-10 result remains below BP (44.46% versus 48.23%), and the asymmetric AGT model achieves only 30.94%. Deep convolutional training is left unexplored, limiting the significance of the broad practicality claims.

Residual ablations do not isolate improved credit assignment from changes in architecture and capacity. Adding skip connections changes both forward computation and feedback paths, without corresponding BP/FA baselines using the same topology or separate forward-only and feedback-only skip ablations.

The BP-equivalence derivation is narrower than the claims suggest: Appendix C assumes infinitesimal feedback and nudging, symmetric feedback weights, and introduces layer-dependent normalization absent from the implemented update. It does not establish gradient correctness for finite feedback, fixed asymmetric connections, or arbitrary residual graphs. First-batch cosine similarities provide useful diagnostics but do not establish equivalence throughout training.

The hardware and biological conclusions exceed the evidence. No physical implementation is evaluated, and the paper itself demonstrates that weak credit signals suffer from float32 precision limitations and increasing sensitivity to state noise with depth. These findings require a more qualified account of practical hardware suitability.

Algorithmic specification needs correction. Section 3.2 says feedback weights remain fixed while other passages require symmetry with changing forward weights. Algorithm S3 resets nudged states inside every iteration, which would prevent the intended settling if followed literally. These ambiguities hinder reproduction of the central method.
